list.listitem: Patients with a solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN) on CXR should have a chest CT without contrast to better characterize the nodule. B
Patients with benign calcification or no change in the nodule in 2 years do not warrant further evaluation. B

Patients who are marginal surgical candidates who have a nodule greater than 1 cm should undergo PET scanning. If PET is negative, follow-up CT should be obtained at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months. B Percutaneous lung biopsy can also be considered for patients with nodules of this size. B
Patients who are operable candidates with a moderate to high clinical suspicion for cancer should have a wedge resection followed by a lobectomy if positive for cancer. B

background.definition: A solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN) is radiologically defined as an intraparenchymal lung lesion that is less than 3 cm in diameter without associated atelectasis, pleural effusions, or adenopathy. Pulmonary nodules can be characterized as solid or subsolid. Subsolid nodules can be further subiivided into partial or full groundglass appearance, in which there is opacification of a higher density than the surrounding tissue but not obscuring underlying bronchovascular structures. SPN can also be indeterminate, where both the pattern of calcification or other features indicate a benign etiology. Lesions greater than 3 cm are called lung masses.

list.listitem: 150,000 new nodules are detected each year.

In a study of incidental pulmonary nodules found during serial CT scanning for follow up endovascular exclusion of abdominal aortic aneurysms, pulmonary lesions were found in 25 patients (18%). Five (4%) died during follow-up; 13 (9%) had stable, subcentimeter lesions; and 6 patients (4%) who underwent biopsy of the lesion were diagnosed with cancer (most stage 1).
Incidence of positive results in participants in low dose CT scanning for lung cancer screening have ranged from 8.2% to 51% in smokers aged 55 to 70 years.

Based on data from the National Lung Screening Trial, the incidence of new solid nodules on postbaseline annual screening exams was 2.6%. Of these new nodules, about half were <6 mm and 17.1% were over 10 mm. While lung cancer risk was higher for larger nodules (1.1% for nodules <4 mm and 24.0% for nodules ≥20 mm), smaller new nodules were more likely to be cancerous than small nodules detected at baseline and larger new nodules were less likely to be cancerous than large nodules identified at baseline.

The incidence of new subsolid tumors in the International Early Lung Cancer Action Project, screening 64,677 individuals, was 0.8% on annual repeat screenings of which 5.2% were stage I lung cancers; most new nodules (69.7%) resolved or decreased in size on subsequent testing.
One in every 500 chest radiographs demonstrates a lung nodule.
The American College of Radiology (ACR) notes that reported frequencies of incidental pulmonary nodules range from 5.6% to 51% on CT and 0.1% to 7% on chest radiographs.
Roughly 1% of solitary pulmonary nodules incidentally found on CT are malignant.
Prevalence of SPN in patients screened with CT for coronary artery calcifications was 18%.

In low-dose CT screening studies for lung cancer among high-risk patients, more than 20% of participants were found on their first scan to have one or more lung nodules that required further investigation. The proportion undergoing invasive diagnostic procedures ranged from 1% to 4%. In a recent retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing lung cancer screening using low-dose CT, one patient in 7 had an abnormality found, but 90% of these findings were not cancer. Screening prompted additional imaging in almost one-third of patients and 2.8% of all screened patients subsequently underwent an invasive procedure.

In the Pan Canadian Early Detection of Lung Cancer Study, 1871 of the 2537 participants (73.7%) had a total of 7008 nodules with 102 patients having nodules that were malignant (5.5%). In the validation dataset from the British Columbia Cancer Agency, 1090 participants had 5021 nodules with 40 patients having lung cancer (3.7%).

Of lung cancers identified by low-dose CT screening, however, about 1 in 5 likely represent overdiagnosis as these cancers are slow-growing and would not cause symptoms or harm during an average 6.4 years of follow-up.

In the International Early Lung Cancer Action Project, subsolid nodules were identified in 5% of baseline screening studies of which 19% resolved at follow-up and 79 cases (2.7%) were diagnosed with stage I lung cancer.
See Differential Diagnosis table.

Nodules in tobacco users, larger nodules, nodules with thicker cavitary walls, and nodules in older patients are more likely to represent malignancy. In a large series from 1987, 22% of SPNs were malignant. However, as smaller nodules are detected via CT, this percentage would be expected to decrease.
Odds ratio (OR) for size as a predictor of malignancy in nodules 0 to 1 cm is 0.52, 1.1 to 2.0 cm is 0.74, 2 to 3 cm is 3.7, and >3 cm is 5.2.
OR for cavitary wall thickness and malignancy is 0.07 for ≥4 mm, 0.72 for 5 to 15 mm, and 38.0 for >15 mm.
OR for age as a predictor of malignancy is 1.0 for <50 years, 1.9 for ages 50 to 59 years, 2.6 for ages 6 to 69 years, and 4.2 >70 years.
Female sex, upper lobe location, spiculation, and larger nodule size are associated with lung cancer.

Based on the 2017 Fleischner guidelines, risk factors that confer a >65% risk for malignancy in a patient with a solitary pulmonary nodule include older age, heavy smoking, prior cancer, larger size, irregular margin, and upper lobe location.

Because data confirm that yearly low-dose CT screening for lung cancer reduces mortality, the United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends annual screening of adults ages 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years (B recommendation). Screening should be discontinued after 15 years of smoking cessation or if the patient develops a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative lung surgery. Following this recommendation will likely increase the detection of new pulmonary nodules.B

In a retrospective study of 94 patients receiving low-dose CT screening in a community-based hospital, investigators found that 22 (23.4%) did not meet the USPSTF criteria for screening and 72 (40.3%) who met screening recommendations required additional imaging based on the initial scan result.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies with 96,559 patients concluded that low-dose CT screening of smokers to identify asymptomatic lung cancer decreases the risk of dying from lung cancer by 1.8% to 2.2% over the subsequent 5 to 10 years, but not overall mortality. Most of the patients (72%), however, came from two trials, the U.S. National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) and the NELSON trial from the Netherlands, described below.

Based primarily on the NLST, a large good-quality trial on the effectiveness of CT screening of smokers for lung cancer, of 53,000 patients screened yearly for 3 years with an additional 3.5 years of follow-up, there was a 20% decrease in lung cancer-related mortality and a 6.7% decrease in overall mortality.

Among high-risk black individuals screened for lung cancer with low-dose CT, mortality reduction from lung cancer was greater than for other racial groups (hazard ratio [HR], 0.61 vs. 0.86) using data from the NLST.

One recent systematic review also showed that annual lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose chest CT for high-risk individuals reduces lung cancer mortality, with a greater reduction observed in Black participants in clinical trials. Black LCS-eligible patients, however, are being screened at a lower rate than White counterparts, but have similar rates of participation once they have been referred.

In a secondary analysis of data from the NLST, authors found that a combination of smoking abstinence at 15 years and low-dose CT screening resulted in a 38% reduction in lung cancer-specific mortality. Smoking abstinence for 7 years among control subjects was identical to the 20% mortality reduction reported with low-dose CT screening.

In an Italian RCT of 3206 smokers low-dose annual CT screening vs. usual care for 4 years resulted in strong trends in reduction of all-cause mortality (105 vs. 127 deaths per 10,000 person years; rate ratio 0.83; 95% CI, 0.67-1.03) and lung cancer–specific mortality (29.3 vs. 42.1 deaths/10,000 person years; rate ratio 0.70; 0.47-1.03) at 9 years. More cancers were diagnosed during the screening period in those randomized to the intervention group, but similar rates of lung cancers were detected at the end of follow-up (67 and 71, respectively) making overdiagnosis unlikely.

In the most recent Dutch RCT (NELSON) of volume-based, low-dose CT screening with 13,195 men and 2594 women participants, aged 50 to 74 years, those randomized to 4 screens over 5.5 years had a reduced risk of lung-cancer mortality at a mean of 8.8 years follow-up (relative risk [RR] 0.75; 95% CI, 0.62-0.90). This represents an absolute risk reduction of 0.8% and a number needed to screen to prevent 1 lung cancer death of 127.
An additional benefit of screening is that participation in a lung cancer screening program increases the likelihood that an individual will quit smoking in the short-term.

The false positive rate in the NLST at baseline was 26.6% (CI, 26.1%-27.1%) and after baseline was 21.8% (CI, 21.4%-22.2%). In another screening study from 8 academic centers, about half of 4246 current or former smokers accepted screening and over half (59.7%) of those had a positive screen.

Nearly all of the 1257 patients had false positive tests, with only 73 patients (3.5%) having suspicious findings for possible lung cancer and 31 (1.5%) had that diagnosis confirmed within the following year. Standardizing lung cancer screening CT reporting and management recommendations may help to reduce the false positive rate.

Not surprisingly, individuals undergoing lung cancer screening have more invasive follow-up tests based on a national database of commercially insured patients aged 55 to 80 years old. These included bronchoscopy (2%), percutaneous biopsy (1.3%), thoracoscopy (0.94%), and mediastinoscopy (0.23%); 0.38% underwent thoracotomy. In the NLST, 21.7% had additional imaging, which was higher than in this study, but rates of bronchoscopy (1.2%), percutaneous biopsy (0.6%), and thoracoscopy (0.3%) were lower although the rate of thoracotomy was higher (0.8%).

Authors of a systematic review confirmed lung cancer and all-cause mortality benefit for current or former smokers, but at significant risk. These risks included overdiagnosis, death (from invasive procedures), major complications of treatment, and false positive results and their consequences.

Another systematic review found various factors affecting the benefit and harms of low-dose CT screening for lung cancer. These included selection of screen-eligible individuals, quality of imaging and image interpretation, the management of screen-detected findings, and the effectiveness of smoking cessation interventions.

It should be noted that not all trials have demonstrated reduced lung cancer mortality; in the Detection And screening of early lung cancer with Novel imaging Technology trial that enrolled 2450 subjects, at a median of 8.5 years follow-up, lung cancer mortality was 543 per 100,000 person-years in the intervention arm vs. 544 per 100,000 person-years in the control/no screening arm.

Also, in the Danish Lung Cancer Screening Trial enrolling 4,104 participants aged 50 to 70 years who had a minimum 20 pack-years of smoking, there were no differences in lung cancer mortality or all-cause mortality at 5 years between those randomized to five annual low-dose CT scans and no screening (control group) despite more cancers and more early-stage cancers being found in the screening group.
Lung cancer screening costs $52,000 per additional life year and $81,000 per additional QALY, and is cost effective only for current smokers ($43,000/QALY vs. $615,000/AQALY for former smokers).

Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) analysis holds promise for early detection of lung cancer and benefits patients with higher survival. One recent study showed that using a stacked ensemble model of cfDNA fragmentomics achieved superior sensitivity for detecting early-stage lung cancer, which could promote early diagnosis and benefit more patients.

Differential.Differential_Name: Primary lung neoplasm (small cell or non small cell)

list.listitem: Patients are generally asymptomatic. 90% are incidental findings, found unexpectedly in radiographs or CT scans obtained for unrelated diagnostic workups.
History of smoking (OR 2.3), asbestos exposure, radon exposure, number of pack-years smoked, and previous malignancy increase likelihood that a nodule is malignant.
All previous CXRs should be reviewed. For all patients with previous CXRs, a spontaneous pulmonary nodule (SPN) that is unchanged for 2 years does not require further diagnostic evaluation.

The ACR (2023) recommends chest CT without IV contrast as usually appropriate for the next imaging study in adults greater than or equal to 35 years of age with incidentally-detected indeterminate pulmonary nodule on chest radiograph and for incidentally-detected indeterminate pulmonary nodule less than 6 mm on chest CT.
One recent study demonstrated that immediate reporting of CXRs from primary care reduced time to diagnosis of lung cancer by half, likely due to a rapid progression to follow up CT.

Chest CT without contrast is the initial imaging modality of choice for the SPN ≥1 cm. It can be useful in identifying nodules more likely to be benign and plays an important role in staging. ACR (2023) recommends either CT chest without IV contrast or FDG-PET/CT whole body as usually appropriate for the next imaging study in adults greater than or equal to 35 years of age with incidentally-detected indeterminate pulmonary nodules equal to or greater than 6 mm on chest CT.
Ultralow dose CT may be as accurate as standard low-dose CT for detecting solid pulmonary nodules >2 mm.

PET scans and helical CT are both accurate tests for patients with solitary pulmonary nodules to distinguish benign from malignant lesions. See for guidance regarding when to use these studies in the diagnostic process. For low-risk patients, the high negative predictive value of a negative PET scan would support observation.

Authors of a meta-analysis of PET scans for diagnosing solitary pulmonary nodules found a sensitivity of 89% (95% confidence interval [CI], 87%-91%), a specificity of 70% (95% CI, 66%-73%), a positive likelihood ratio of 3.33 (95% CI, 2.35-4.71) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.18 (95% CI, 0.13-0.25).
High-risk patients (e.g., older age, previous malignancy, smoking history) should have a tissue diagnosis. Transthoracic needle aspiration has sensitivity for malignancy of 64% to 100%.

The diagnostic yield of bronchoscopy for peripheral lesions is 40% to 80%. The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence suggests that negative or inconclusive specimens obtained using endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial biopsy should be further investigated using other biopsy techniques.

The best use of bronchoscopy and transbronchial needle aspiration is for staging of non-small cell lung cancer by aspirating enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. Preoperative bronchoscopy is unlikely to change management.

CT scan-guided transthoracic core-needle biopsy for lung nodules had an estimated sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 89%, 99%, and 90%, respectively in a review of 980 specimens from 3 centers. The complication rate was 34% with life-threatening complications in 6%. In two recent studies of CT scan-guided percutaneous cutting needle biopsy of 141 and 248 lung nodules <20 mm, malignancy was identified in 64% and 73.1%, respectively. In the former study, sensitivity, specificity, and overall diagnostic accuracy were 94.4%, 100%, and 96.1% and diagnostic accuracy in the latter study was 96.8%. The most common complication in both studies was pneumothorax occurring in 12.1% and 16.1%.

Diagnosis through robot-assisted lobectomy (RAL) is increasingly used as an alternative to video-assisted lobectomy (VAL) for resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). And one recent study found that both RAL and VAL showed satisfactory and comparable health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and postoperative pain up to 48 weeks after surgery.
Another recent study showed RAL achieved similar perioperative outcomes, together with higher LN yield in NSCLC.

In operable patients with a SPN, surgical resection is the ideal approach, as it is both diagnostic and therapeutic. If the lesion is amenable to a wedge resection, then it is the procedure of choice followed by a lobectomy if the pathologic finding is positive for cancer. For patients with an SPN who are not operable candidates, transthoracic needle aspiration may be helpful to establish tissue diagnosis.
All pulmonary resections must include a systematic lymph node dissection.
For patients with a SPN who are marginal surgical candidates, a wedge resection or segmentectomy is acceptable.
Serum concentrations of biomarkers of angiogenesis and those related to insulin-like growth factor may be useful in distinguishing stage 1 non-small cell lung cancers from benign nodules.
Epidermal growth factor receptor gene mutations found in resected lung adenocarcinoma serve as a risk factor for poor prognosis and can be used in staging surgically-resected lung adenocarcinoma.
Aclinical decision rule has been developed and validated to predict the probability of malignancy in patients who present with a pulmonary nodule.
It includes the patient's age, the size, location and characteristics of the nodule, and whether they smoke or have had cancer. Optionally the rule can also include PET scan findings.

Using datasets from two national studies of low-dose CT screening for lung cancer among high-risk patients, two models were developed to predict lung cancer in pulmonary nodules. In the first, female sex, upper lobe location, spiculation, and larger nodule size in a nonlinear relationship, were associated with lung cancer. In the second model, including more factors, older age, emphysema, family history of lung cancer, lower nodule count, and part-solid nodule appearance were also linked to greater likelihood of malignancy.

Because the differentiation of primary lung cancers and pulmonary metastases can present with overlapping CT findings, one recent study aimed to compare the utility of ringlike peripheral increased iodine concentration and conventional findings for differentiating primary lung cancers from pulmonary metastases on dual-energy CT (DECT). Ringlike peripheral high iodine concentration had excellent interobserver agreement and high specificity, but poor sensitivity for differentiating pulmonary metastasis from primary lung cancer and was independently predictive of pulmonary metastasis.
For patients with a SPN that is visible on the CXR, all previous CXRs should be reviewed. C
For all patients with previous CXRs, an SPN that is unchanged for 2 years does not require further diagnostic evaluation. B
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the SPN.

Based on the 2017 Fleischner guidelines, patients at low risk of malignancy (e.g., young, non-smoker or little tobacco use, no prior cancer, regular margins and non-upper lobe location) with a single <6 mm nodule of any type do not require follow-up.

If a low-risk patient has a solid nodule >8 mm, they should undergo a CT scan at 3 months, PET/CT or biopsy. For groundglass appearing nodules, a 3-month CT is recommended to confirm persistence and then a CT in 3 to 5 years. If the lesion is subsolid and a 3-month CT confirms persistence, annual CTs for 5 years is recommended.

High-risk patients with a single solid nodule of <6 mm should be given the option of a follow-up CT in one year. For solid nodules 6 to 8 mm, a CT at 6 to 12 months is recommended with a follow-up at 18 to 24 months if no change. For larger nodules, consider a CT scan at 3 months, PET/CT or biopsy.

Order chest CT (no old films are available, or the nodule is not present or is smaller on prior films).

Does the nodule have a (1) laminated or central pattern of calcification (typical of granulomas), (2) a "popcorn" pattern of calcification (seen in hamartomas), or (3) fat and cartilage (seen in hamartomas)? Spiculated.
Is patient high risk (age >50, history of malignancy, smoking history, speculated nodule, or upper lobe nodule)?
To OR for wedge resection and if malignant, lobectomy.
PET scan or percutaneous lung biopsy.
Either refer to interventional radiologist for transthoracic needle biopsy if the lesion is peripheral, or refer to pulmonologist for bronchoscopy if the lesion is proximal.
6-8 mm. Repeat CT at 6-12 months and then at 18-24 months.
